issues.issue: The parenthetical defining B-4 Partners LLC is never closed — it reads ("Managers Fund and Manager each being referred to individually as a "Borrower" — so the instrument never cleanly assigns the defined term "Manager" to B-4 Partners. A court asked who the "Manager" is, and whether the joint-and-several designation attaches to both entities, would have to repair the punctuation.

The 10%-ownership, director and joint-venture deeming rules in clauses (a)-(c) are expressly confined to "the definition of Eligible Notes Receivable and Section 7.13", so everywhere else in the agreement (e.g. the Schedule 5.21 representation that no Approved Title Insurance Company is an Affiliate, and Section 8.9) only the narrower "control" test applies. Whether a 10% holder is an "Affiliate" therefore depends on which provision is being applied, an expressio unius problem on the face of the definition.

The premium is measured by a percentage of the Maximum Revolver Amount ($50,000,000) rather than of amounts actually outstanding, so a borrower who never drew the line owes the same $500,000 as one fully drawn. Whether that is a reasonable estimate of loss or an unenforceable penalty is a construction question on the definition's own terms.

The definition closes with the open-ended catch-all "together with any obligations undertaken or assumed relating thereto", which has no stated boundary against the two specific categories that precede it (obligations to withdrawing members and Subordinated Notes). Because Approved Debt is both Permitted Indebtedness (7.1(e)) and secured by Permitted Liens (clause (c)), the reach of that catch-all determines what other debt the Fund may incur.

The definition says Lender's approval of an additional title company "will not be unreasonably withheld" but in the same sentence gives Lender the right "in its reasonable discretion" to remove any company from the list. The two standards sit against each other and leave it unclear whether a company approved on a not-unreasonably-withheld basis can be removed at will.

The three alternatives are not commensurable: clause (a) requires a FIRREA-compliant appraisal, while clause (c) accepts "an informal or unwritten estimate of value by Servicer". Because clause (c) swallows clause (a), what an "Authorized Appraisal" must be — and therefore what supports Note Receivable valuations — is indeterminate on the face of the definition.

After naming five individuals the definition adds "or such other Person serving at such time as the Chief Financial Officer of Manager", a catch-all that neither identifies a CFO nor says whether the named individuals cease to be Authorized Persons on leaving. Since Section 2.8 lets Lender fund on instructions from "anyone purporting to be an Authorized Person", the boundary of the class matters.

"Bank Product" opens with the unbounded phrase "any financial accommodation extended to any Borrower ... including" and then lists seven specific services, so it is unclear whether the enumerated items limit the general words (ejusdem generis) or merely illustrate them. Because Bank Product Obligations are secured by all Collateral and share the payment waterfall, the reach of the general phrase is consequential.

The Bank Product Reserve is deducted from the Borrowing Base under clause (b)(i) of the "Borrowing Base" definition, separately from the Section 2.1(b) reserves, so it appears to escape the promise in Section 2.1(b) that Lender "will not establish any such reserves unless a Triggering Event has occurred". Whether Lender may shrink availability by a Bank Product Reserve absent a Triggering Event cannot be answered from either provision alone.

The rate is whatever Lender determines "in accordance with its customary procedures" using "such electronic or other quotation sources as it considers appropriate", and the determination is "conclusive in the absence of manifest error" — a term the agreement never defines. What counts as manifest error, and whether the customary-procedures standard is judicially reviewable, is left open.

The definition concedes that the "prime rate" is "not necessarily the lowest" of Wells Fargo's base rates and is proved by internal publications Wells Fargo designates, so the index is set unilaterally by the lender's affiliate. Whether "prime rate" carries any objective content is a question on the face of the definition.

"[A]ny reference in this Agreement to a Borrower shall be a reference to each of and either of Fund and Manager" is self-contradictory: "each of" makes every covenant a covenant of both, while "either of" makes it satisfiable by one. Read against the joint-and-several provisions of Section 2.13 and the consolidation rule in Section 1.2, which reading governs a given covenant is genuinely uncertain.

The definition grants "all property, including, without limitation, each of the following" and then enumerates twelve categories that omit Real Property from the granting list while including it only among proceeds. Whether the general words carry owned Real Property (including Real Estate Owned) into the Borrower Collateral, or whether the enumeration limits them, is a general-versus-specific problem in the words themselves.

The Required Procedures are an unattached extrinsic writing — "in the form delivered to Lender and approved by Lender prior to the Closing Date" — yet eligibility of every Note Receivable, and Sections 6.5, 7.9 and 4.8, turn on them. Identifying the operative version of that document is a construction problem the definition itself creates.

The certificate is required to list "all Real Estate Owned as of the date thereof", but Real Estate Owned appears nowhere in the Borrowing Base formula in the definition of "Borrowing Base". Why the certificate that is "used to determine the Borrowing Base" must carry an item the formula ignores is unresolved between the two definitions.

"Business Day" is fixed by bank closings in New York or California, yet every operative deadline in the agreement is stated in Dallas (Texas) time — Sections 2.2(a), 2.3(a), 2.7 and 2.12(b). A Texas bank holiday that is not a New York or California holiday leaves the two provisions pulling against each other on when a payment or borrowing request is timely.

Clauses (a) and (b) make it a Change of Control if Manager ceases to be sole manager of Fund or if the four Permitted Holders cease to own 100% of Manager, yet the definition of "Permitted Reorganization" expressly contemplates "the admission to the Fund of Manager and/or Servicer and their affiliates as members, managing members or managers". Whether a Permitted Reorganization can be carried out without tripping Section 7.8 cannot be answered from either definition alone.

"Code" means the New York UCC except that, for attachment, perfection, priority or remedies governed by another state's mandatory law, it means that state's UCC "solely for purposes of the provisions thereof relating to such attachment, perfection, priority, or remedies". Because a long list of collateral terms (Account, Deposit Account, Equipment, Inventory, Investment Property) is defined by reference to "the Code", which state's definition applies to a given asset is left uncertain.

"Collections" is defined as "all cash, checks, notes, instruments, and other items of payment" with no limitation as to whose payments or on what account, so read literally it captures every dollar the Borrowers receive from any source. Section 2.6(a) then requires all of "their Collections" to be deposited within one Business Day, making the unbounded definition operative.

The certificate must be "delivered by the chief financial officer of Administrative Borrower", but the agreement nowhere establishes that Manager has a chief financial officer — Section 3.2(a) instead requires a Controller to be hired within 120 days, and Exhibit C-1 is signed simply by "the undersigned officer of Manager". Who may validly deliver a Compliance Certificate is left unresolved between the definition and Exhibit C-1.

A note becomes a "Defaulted Note Receivable" if "Administrative Borrower or Lender deems" it non-performing or non-collectible — a purely subjective test, exercisable by either party, with no standard of reasonableness attached. Because Section 7.17 caps Defaulted and Delinquent Notes at 25% of the portfolio, one party's unilateral "deeming" can manufacture or avoid an Event of Default.

Delinquency is measured against the note's original terms "or as extended in accordance with Borrower's Required Procedures", so the Borrower can reset the ninety-day clock by extending under procedures it drafts. Whether an extension cures delinquency for purposes of Section 7.17 turns on that open-ended qualifier.

The eligibility criteria "may be modified from time to time by Lender in Lender's Permitted Discretion", and any excluded note may nonetheless be treated as eligible "by the Lender following a review thereof on a case-by-case basis" — so the twenty-one enumerated exclusions do not in fact fix the class. What is an Eligible Note Receivable, and hence the Borrowing Base, is left to be settled by the lender's own say-so.

Clause (a) excludes every note that does not evidence a commercial loan "which loan was originated by Servicer but is now held by Fund", while the definition of "Note Receivable" covers a note evidencing "a loan made or purchased by Fund". Purchased loans are Notes Receivable but can never be eligible, and the two definitions cannot both be given full effect.

"Executive Officer" is defined as five named individuals without reference to any office, yet Section 8.13 makes it a default if an Executive Officer "cease[s] to be employed in his current position with Manager or Servicer". Which position each named person holds, and whether the definition even presupposes employment, is left to be filled in from outside the instrument.

Clause (d) sweeps in "all obligations or liabilities of others secured by a Lien on any asset of a Person ... irrespective of whether such obligation or liability is assumed", which on its face makes third-party debt the Borrower's own Indebtedness for purposes of the Section 7.1 prohibition. How far that non-recourse category extends is not bounded by anything in the definition.

An Interest Period is fixed as a calendar month running from the first day to the last day of that month, but Section 2.12(a) offers the LIBOR Option on "all of the Advances" and Advances may be funded on any Business Day. How interest is determined on an Advance made mid-month, and whether it can ever be a LIBOR Rate Loan before the next month begins, is unresolved between this definition and Section 2.12.

The term is defined as "an interest in a member's interest in Fund", a double-nesting that leaves it unclear whether an Investor Membership Interest is the member's own LLC interest or some derivative participation in it. Sections 5.20, 7.10, 7.14 and 8.9 all turn on the term.

Clauses (i) and (j) make reimbursable Lender's costs "incurred in advising, structuring, drafting, reviewing, administering, or amending the Loan Documents" and in "defending the Loan Documents, irrespective of whether suit is brought", with no reasonableness qualifier on several of the enumerated categories while others carry one. Which charges are recoverable as Lender Expenses — and therefore chargeable to the Loan Account as Advances under Section 2.5(c) — is uncertain on the face of the list.

The definition expressly includes "reservations, exceptions, encroachments, easements, rights-of-way, covenants, conditions, restrictions, leases, and other title exceptions ... affecting Real Property", so Section 7.2's flat prohibition on suffering any Lien to exist would be breached by ordinary title exceptions on every parcel. Only clause (k) of "Permitted Liens" rescues some of them, and whether the two can be read together is not answerable from this definition alone.

After enumerating specific instruments the definition adds "any other agreement entered into, now or in the future, by any Borrower and Lender in connection with this Agreement", so the class of Loan Documents is open-ended. Because Section 8.2 makes breach of any "comparable provision contained in any of the other Loan Documents" an Event of Default, the reach of that catch-all determines the reach of the default clause.

"Material Adverse Change" turns on a "material adverse change in the business, prospects, operations, results of operations, assets, liabilities or financial condition" — with "prospects" and "material" left undefined and no baseline or measurement period stated. The term controls the funding condition in Section 3.3(d) and several representations, so its boundary is squarely contestable.

The $50,000,000 ceiling cannot be reconciled with Section 7.16(b), which caps the Senior Leverage Ratio — Obligations over Tangible Net Worth — at nine-tenths of one percent, permitting only about $5.4 million of Obligations against the $600,000,000 Tangible Net Worth required by Section 3.1(n). Drawing anywhere near the Maximum Revolver Amount would breach the covenant on the first testing date.

The parenthetical "(less portions that are not in compliance with the definition thereof)" subtracts from a quantity already limited to Eligible Notes Receivable, which by definition comply. Whether the parenthetical adds a further haircut, or is mere surplusage, is an ambiguity in the definition's own words.

"New Fund" is keyed to entities formed "after the Effective Date", a term this Agreement never defines — the operative date elsewhere is the "Closing Date", and Section 16.1 speaks only of when the Agreement is "deemed effective". The further requirement that the entity be "funded principally using debt securities" and not "capitalized or otherwise funded with assets of such Borrower" supplies no measurement point either.

Any New Fund is carved out of the definition of "Subsidiary", which means the Section 7.13 prohibition on forming or acquiring a Subsidiary without Lender's consent, and the Section 7.12 restriction on Investments, do not reach it. Whether the Borrowers could form and deal with an affiliated lending fund free of those covenants can only be decided by reading this definition with Sections 7.12 and 7.13.

A Note Receivable is a note evidencing a loan "made or purchased by Fund", but clause (a) of the "Eligible Notes Receivable" definition excludes any loan not "originated by Servicer but ... now held by Fund". The two provisions describe different populations, and which one governs a purchased loan for reporting and eligibility purposes is unresolved.

The definition — "the real property securing an Eligible Note Receivable in which Fund has a title-insured first priority lien, or security title to, that has been assigned or pledged to Lender" — is grammatically broken, so it is unclear whether "that has been assigned or pledged" modifies the real property, the lien, or the Note Receivable. What must have been assigned to Lender before property qualifies as Note Receivable Collateral is therefore uncertain.

"Offering Circular" lumps together the Private Offering Memorandum "as amended from time to time", the LLC operating agreement, subscription agreements and unspecified "related agreements and instruments". Because Section 5.3 warrants that "[a]ny Offering Circular" complies with all applicable securities laws, the open-ended composition of the term fixes the scope of that representation.

"Permitted Discretion" is defined as "reasonable (from the perspective of a secured asset-based lender) business judgment" — a standard measured from one party's own vantage point and nowhere further specified. The term governs reserves, eligibility criteria, Additional Documents, consent to modifications and the materiality judgment in Section 8.16, so its content is repeatedly decisive.

Only clause (e) — sales of Notes Receivable — carries the condition that proceeds be paid directly into a Cash Management Account, while clauses (f) and (g) permit sales of Note Receivable Collateral and of Real Estate Owned with no such condition. Whether the cash-management requirement of Section 2.6(a) nonetheless reaches those proceeds is left open by the enumeration.

Clause (c)'s parenthetical is broken — "so long as such Liens for Approved Debt or subordinated to the Liens held by Lender on the terms approved by Lender as part of a Permitted Reorganization" — leaving no verb and no discernible condition. Whether Liens securing Approved Debt must actually be subordinated, and on whose terms, cannot be read off the clause as written.

A reorganization qualifies only if it "is consistent in all material respects with the written description provided to Lender by Borrowers prior to the Closing Date" — an extrinsic, unattached and unidentified writing that Section 16.10's integration clause does not incorporate. Whether a particular restructuring was a Permitted Reorganization therefore cannot be determined from the four corners of the instrument.

"Real Property" is defined as real property owned or acquired "by a Borrower or any of its Subsidiaries", yet clauses (b) and (h) of the "Eligible Notes Receivable" definition require each note to be secured by a first-priority Lien on "Real Property" — that is, on property the maker owns, not the Borrower. Applying the defined term where it is used makes the eligibility criteria impossible to satisfy.

Clause (e) sweeps in "any payment ... by Borrower to a holder of Stock in a Borrower or to an Affiliate ... not expressly authorized in this Agreement", which makes the definition circular: whether a payment is a Restricted Payment depends on whether the Agreement authorizes it, and Section 7.10 authorizes it only if it is not a Restricted Payment. Ordinary redemptions of Investor Membership Interests fall in that circle.

The definition states a plain ratio of Obligations to Tangible Net Worth, but Section 7.16(b) tests that ratio "expressed as a percentage" against nine-tenths of one percent, a figure that on any $600,000,000 Tangible Net Worth allows only about $5.4 million of Obligations. Whether the covenant means 0.9 or 90% cannot be settled from the definition alone.

The definition covers "an Approved Title Insurance Company or any settlement agent (including a title company, title agency, attorney or law firm covered by a Closing Protection Letter issued by an Approved Title Insurance Company)", and it is unclear whether the Closing Protection Letter requirement qualifies every settlement agent or only the parenthetical examples. Section 6.18 requires all initial disbursements to go through a Settlement Agent, so the scope matters.

"Solvent" is reduced to a single balance-sheet test — "at fair valuations, the sum of such Person's assets is greater than all of such Person's debts" — with no definition of "debts", no treatment of contingent or unliquidated liabilities, and none of the usual capital-adequacy or ability-to-pay prongs. Section 5.12(a) and clause (q) of the eligibility criteria both turn on the term.

A Subordinated Note is described as "secured by the assets of Fund", but clause (a) of the definition of "Subordinated Debt" admits only "unsecured Indebtedness", and clause (b) admits Approved Debt, which Subordinated Notes evidence. Whether a secured Subordinated Note is Subordinated Debt — and hence added back into Tangible Net Worth — cannot be squared between the two definitions.

The proviso excludes from "Subsidiary" any post-Closing entity not capitalized with a Borrower's assets, any New Fund, and Bar-K, Inc., which leaves the first sentence of Section 7.13 — "Form or acquire any Subsidiary without the prior written consent of Lender" — with almost nothing to operate on. Whether the covenant reaches a newly formed affiliated fund depends entirely on reading the two together.

Clause (b) is triggered when "the aggregate outstanding principal amount of all Notes Receivable of Fund is less than $500,000,000" without saying whether that measures eligible notes, notes net of write-downs, or gross face amount. Because Section 2.1(b) makes the Triggering Event the switch for Lender's reserve rights, how the portfolio is measured is decisive.

The direction that "Borrower" in a financial covenant means "Fund and its Subsidiaries on a consolidated basis" cannot be squared with the definition of "Senior Leverage Ratio", which takes "the outstanding amount of all Obligations of Borrower" — Obligations that Section 2.13 makes the joint and several debt of both Fund and Manager. Whether Manager's borrowings enter the covenant calculation is left to the escape hatch "unless the context clearly requires otherwise".

The last sentence provides that "[a]ny requirement of a writing contained herein or in the other Loan Documents shall be satisfied by the transmission of a Record", which sits against Section 15.1's requirement that amendments and waivers "be in writing and signed by Lender and Administrative Borrower". Whether an electronic Record can effect an amendment or waiver is unresolved between the two.

This section incorporates all schedules by reference, while Section 6.14 provides that no notification "shall ... have the effect of amending or modifying this Agreement or any of the Schedules hereto" — yet Schedules 5.5, 5.8, 5.16, 5.18 and 5.21 are each described in the text as "updated from time to time" and Sections 6.9 and 2.6(c) expressly let the Borrowers amend schedules. Which incorporated version of a schedule governs is not answerable from this section alone.

Lender "agrees to make advances" up to the lesser of the Maximum Revolver Amount and the Borrowing Base, but Sections 2.1(b), 2.1(c) and 2.1(e) and the conditions in Section 3.3 (including the undefined "Material Adverse Change") leave Lender with no enforceable obligation to fund. Whether the commitment in 2.1(a) has content once those provisions are read with it is a whole-instrument question.

The section gives Lender an open right to establish reserves and then promises "not to establish any such reserves unless a Triggering Event has occurred and is continuing", yet Section 10 authorizes Lender, whenever a Borrower fails to pay a third party, to "set up such reserves against the Borrowing Base or the Maximum Revolver Amount as Lender deems necessary" with no Triggering Event condition. The two cannot both be given full effect.

The second limit caps availability plus cash in the Cash Management Accounts at "the aggregate amount of unfunded commitments of Fund to the makers of Notes Receivable", a quantity the agreement never defines, never requires to be reported, and never ties to the Borrowing Base Certificate. How that ceiling is computed, and by whom, is left open.

The notice must be received "no later than noon (Dallas time) on the Business Day that is the requested Funding Date", yet "Business Day" is defined by New York and California bank closings, and the sentence allowing telephonic notice "[a]t Lender's election" leaves it unclear whether the Borrower or the Lender chooses the form of request. Both points bear on whether a given request obliges Lender to fund.

This subsection disapplies the whole Section 2.3(b) waterfall to "any payment made by Borrowers to Lender and specified by Borrowers to be for the payment of specific Obligations then due and payable", which lets the Borrowers reorder the priorities that Section 2.3(b)(i) fixes. Whether a borrower-directed payment overrides the first-to-Lender-Expenses ordering is a conflict between the two subsections.

The conflict rule is confined to "the priority provisions of this Section 2.3" and to conflicts "contained in any other Loan Document", so it resolves nothing about conflicts within this Agreement itself — for example between Section 2.1(b) and Section 10 on reserves. Naming one category of conflict and no other invites an expressio unius reading.

An Overadvance arises whenever Obligations exceed "any of the limitations set forth in Section 2.1", which includes Section 2.1(c)'s cap tied to the Fund's unfunded loan commitments — a figure the agreement never defines or requires to be reported. The Borrowers' duty to repay "immediately" is triggered by a limit whose amount they cannot compute from the instrument.

The default rate is four points above "the per annum rate otherwise applicable to Base Rate Loans" even as to Advances that are LIBOR Rate Loans, and it applies only "at the election of Lender" with no mechanism for making or communicating that election. When and at what rate default interest begins to run is left uncertain.

Interest, fees and Lender Expenses are charged to the Loan Account and "thereafter shall constitute Advances hereunder", but Section 2.1(c) forbids Revolver Usage from exceeding the Maximum Revolver Amount and Section 2.4 makes any excess an immediately repayable Overadvance. Whether Lender's own charges can create a borrower default under those caps is not resolved by either provision.

Clause (ii) requires all Collections to be deposited into a Cash Management Account "in Fund's name", yet Section 2.6(e) and Section 6.17 require escrow monies — including amounts held for Account Debtors — to go into Escrow Accounts, and Section 2.6(e) excepts "accounts belonging to an Account Debtor of Borrower" while Section 6.17 does not. Where funds held for a third party must be deposited cannot be answered from this subsection alone.

Clause (iii) requires each Cash Management Bank to "forward by daily sweep all amounts in the applicable Cash Management Account to the Lender's Account", which cannot be squared with Section 2.6(e)'s permission for Borrower to withdraw escrow funds daily or with Section 2.1(c)(B), which assumes a continuing "aggregate balance of cash in the Cash Management Accounts". A daily total sweep leaves nothing for either provision to operate on.

This subsection makes the Cash Management Accounts "subject to Control Agreements", but Section 2.6(b) requires those same accounts to be governed by "Cash Management Agreements" — a separately defined term with different required provisions. Which agreement must be in place for a Cash Management Account, and whether both are required, is unresolved between the two subsections.

The subsection creates a deposit account defined as the "Escrow Account" and then, in the very next sentences, imposes requirements on "such Cash Management Account" and its deposits, so it is unclear whether an Escrow Account is a Cash Management Account subject to the daily sweep in Section 2.6(b). The Borrower's stated right to withdraw escrow funds daily depends on which label controls.

Lender is authorized to advance "based upon telephonic or other instructions received from anyone purporting to be an Authorized Person", allocating to Borrowers the risk of an impostor without any verification duty or callback procedure. Whether that phrase covers an unauthorized person whom Lender had reason to doubt is left open.

Loan Account statements become "conclusively presumed to be correct" and an account stated unless objected to within 30 days, "absent manifest error" — a term the agreement never defines. What kind of error escapes the conclusive presumption is the whole question in any dispute over the balance owed.

The fee rate is written as "one-half of one percent (0.30%) per annum" — the words and the numeral state two different rates, and elsewhere the agreement equates one-half of one percent with 0.50%. A court would have to decide which controls, and the clause's final cross-reference "(v) $20,000,000" does not match the (i)/(ii)/(A) lettering of the sentence.

The minimum interest charge deems the average Daily Balance to have been $20,000,000, and Section 2.10(c) separately charges an unused line fee computed on the excess of the Maximum Revolver Amount over the greater of the actual average balance "or $20,000,000 during the Minimum Interest Period". Whether the two provisions together charge twice for the same undrawn $20,000,000 is not resolved by either.

The capital-adequacy charge is triggered by a reduction in return "by any amount deemed by Lender to be material", calculated by Lender using "any reasonable averaging and attribution methods", and the resulting statement is "deemed true and correct absent manifest error". None of those standards is defined, so the amount payable rests on the Lender's own determination.

This subsection offers the option only to have interest "on all of the Advances" determined by the LIBOR Rate, while Section 2.12(b) speaks of an election "for a permitted portion of the Advances". Whether the Borrowers may split the loan between Base Rate and LIBOR tranches cannot be answered without choosing between the two subsections.

The notice provision contemplates an election "for a permitted portion of the Advances and an Interest Period", but Section 2.12(a) and the deemed-election rule in Section 2.12(c) both operate on an all-or-nothing basis covering "all of the Advances", and nothing in the agreement says what portions are "permitted". The two subsections cannot both be given effect.

This subsection deems the LIBOR Option elected for every Interest Period unless the Borrower opts out, whereas Section 2.12(a) provides that at the end of an Interest Period a LIBOR Rate Loan "automatically shall convert" to the Base Rate "unless Administrative Borrower properly has exercised the LIBOR Option". The default setting is opposite in the two subsections.

Lender may terminate the LIBOR Option whenever, "in the reasonable opinion of Lender", any change in market conditions makes it "unlawful or impractical" to fund or maintain LIBOR Rate Loans — "impractical" and "change in market conditions" being nowhere defined, and Section 2.12(e) confirming that Lender need not match-fund at all. What circumstances suffice is left to the Lender's opinion.

The subsection makes each Borrower's obligations absolute "irrespective of the validity, regularity or enforceability of this Agreement or any other circumstances whatsoever", which purports to survive the unenforceability of the very instrument creating the obligation. It also cross-refers to "this Section 2.15", a section that does not exist in the agreement.

The waiver is framed entirely in terms of "Section 580(d) of the California Code of Civil Procedure", yet Section 13(a) provides that construction, interpretation and enforcement of this Agreement are "GOVERNED BY ... THE LAWS OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK". Whether a New York-governed contract can waive California antideficiency protections, and what the clause means if California law does not apply, cannot be settled without reading the two together.

This waiver of "all rights and defenses that such Borrower may have because the Obligations are secured by Real Property" presupposes the California one-action and antideficiency regime, while Section 13(a) makes New York law govern the Agreement. The clause's operative content depends on which state's law supplies the rights being waived.

Clause (B) provides that "Agent and Lenders may collect from such Borrower", but this is a bilateral agreement with a single "Lender" and no "Agent" — neither term is defined here. Who holds the right the clause confers, and whether it operates at all, is a defect in the clause's own words.

The condition requires Lender to have completed a sprawling list of diligence items "the results of which shall be satisfactory to Lender", with no standard of reasonableness and no deemed-satisfaction mechanism. Read with the preamble's statement that funding is "conclusively deemed" satisfaction or waiver, whether the condition ever had content is contestable.

Reference checks on four named individuals must produce results "satisfactory to Lender in its sole discretion", a standard that appears nowhere else among the Section 3.1 conditions, which use "satisfactory to Lender" simpliciter. Whether "sole discretion" displaces the good-faith limits implied elsewhere is a question on the face of the clause.

The condition demands that Borrowers actually hold all required licenses and be "in compliance with any applicable federal or state statutes or regulations regarding Fund's offering, sale or redemption of the Investor Membership Interests", and then dissolves that demand with a proviso that it "may be satisfied by Fund providing to Lender such reasonable assurances as Lender may require". A promise of assurances is not compliance, and the two halves of the clause pull apart.

The eight documents listed here for the initial $250,000,000 of pledged notes do not match the nine-item list in clause (r) of the "Eligible Notes Receivable" definition, which additionally requires evidence of casualty insurance and a recorded collateral assignment. Because Section 3.3(e) and Section 8.17 both police the $250,000,000 pool by reference to "the documents required by Section 3.1(t)", the discrepancy between the two lists is operative.

After twenty enumerated conditions the section closes with "all other documents and legal matters in connection with the transactions contemplated by this Agreement shall have been delivered, executed, or recorded and shall be in form and substance satisfactory to Lender". Whether that catch-all is limited by the specific conditions preceding it, or is a free-standing condition of unlimited scope, is a general-versus-specific problem in the clause itself.

The preamble to Section 3.2 states that failure to satisfy a condition subsequent itself constitutes an Event of Default, while Section 8.2(c) treats "failure to satisfy a condition subsequent set forth in Section 3.2 within the period stated" as a default only if it "continues for a period of 20 Business Days". Whether the Controller-hiring failure defaults the loan at once or after a cure period cannot be answered from either provision alone.

The condition that "no Material Adverse Change shall have occurred" fixes no baseline date against which the change is measured, and the defined term itself reaches "prospects" without further limit. Because this is a condition to every Advance, the absence of a measurement point governs whether Lender may stop funding.

The termination sentence is internally contradictory: it makes Lender's right to terminate "subject to any notice and cure rights otherwise provided by this Agreement" and in the same breath permits termination "immediately and without notice" upon an Event of Default. Whether the cure periods in Section 8.2 must run before termination is left unresolved by the clause's own words.

The clause imposes the prepayment premium as agreed liquidated damages on terminations including "termination upon the election of Lender ... after the occurrence and during the continuation of an Event of Default" and confirmation of a plan of reorganization, but then qualifies the obligation with the undefined words "if applicable". Whether the premium is owed in a bankruptcy plan context, and what "if applicable" refers to, is left open.

This section requires original notes "sufficient to ensure that Lender ... at all times holds Eligible Notes Receivable having an aggregate outstanding principal amount of not less than $250,000,000", yet Section 4.9(a) obliges Lender to return each note on repayment and Section 4.9(b) on sale, which can drop the pool below the floor without any act of the Borrower. How the two are reconciled — and whether Section 8.17's three-day cure is the answer — is not stated here.

Clauses (b), (e) and (f) of the power of attorney are expressly limited to times when an Event of Default has occurred and is continuing, while clauses (c) and (d) — verification inquiries to Account Debtors and endorsement of the Borrower's payment items — carry no such limitation. The enumeration invites an expressio unius reading that Lender may exercise those powers at any time, including before default.

This section lets Lender direct liquidation of Deposit and Securities Accounts "[u]pon the occurrence and during the continuance of a Default or Event of Default", whereas Section 9.1 makes every other remedy available only "[u]pon the occurrence, and during the continuation, of an Event of Default". Whether Lender may seize account balances on a mere Default — an event that by definition has not yet ripened — is a conflict between the two provisions.

Servicing rights may be revoked only "after the occurrence and during the continuation of an Event of Default" and then "by giving notice to Administrative Borrower in accordance with the terms of the Servicing Agreement", while Section 9.1(e) lets Lender "terminate the Servicing Agreement and assign servicing responsibilities to any replacement servicer". Whether the procedures of the Servicing Agreement bind Lender when it acts under Section 9.1 is not resolved here.

The subsection requires Lender to return a repaid note "to Administrative Borrower to facilitate its payment" and to release its Lien "promptly upon receipt of the final payment", although the note is described as already "repaid in its entirety". The sequence — repaid, then returned to facilitate payment, then released on final payment — is internally inconsistent.

Clause (c) warrants that each identified note "is not excluded as ineligible by virtue of one or more of the excluding criteria set forth in the definition of Eligible Notes Receivable", while that definition in turn defines Eligible Notes Receivable as notes "that comply with each of the representations and warranties respecting Eligible Notes Receivable made in the Loan Documents". The two provisions define each other in a circle.

The sentence that "[a]ny Offering Circular ... all Investor Membership Interests issued by Fund, and all aspects of Borrowers' operations, comply with all applicable federal, state and local laws and regulations" is stated without the materiality qualifier that governs the sentences around it and without any knowledge limitation. How absolute a securities-law compliance warranty this creates is a question on its own words.

The representation carves out anything "described on Schedule 5.8 or in an Offering Circular", and "Offering Circular" is defined to include the private offering memorandum "as amended from time to time" together with all subscription agreements. The exception can therefore expand after closing without Lender's assent, so what the Borrower has actually warranted about its capital Stock is indeterminate.

The disclosure warranty is qualified three times by the phrase "(taken as a whole)", which is nowhere defined and leaves it unclear whether a single false statement can breach the representation or only a misleading overall picture. Section 8.11 makes "any material misstatement or misrepresentation" an Event of Default, so the aggregation qualifier is doing real work.

The representation that no listed title company "is an Affiliate of Borrower" must be tested under the definition of "Affiliate", whose expanded 10%-ownership, director and joint-venture rules apply only "for purposes of the definition of Eligible Notes Receivable and Section 7.13 hereof". Which version of "Affiliate" governs this representation is unresolved between the two provisions.

The reporting schedule ends with the open-ended item "(h) such other reports as to the Collateral or the financial condition of each Borrower and its Subsidiaries, as Lender may request", following seven specifically described reports with fixed deadlines. Whether that catch-all is bounded by the enumerated categories — and what deadline attaches to it, given that breach of Section 6.2 is an immediate Event of Default under Section 8.2(a) — is left open.

Clause (c) requires annual statements "certified, without any qualifications (including any (A) 'going concern' or like qualification or exception ...)", so an auditor's going-concern paragraph is itself a breach of covenant and, under Section 8.2(a), an immediate Event of Default with no cure period. Whether the covenant is a reporting obligation or a substantive financial condition is a question on its own words.

The collection covenant stacks three undefined and circular formulations — "use commercially reasonable efforts ... to promptly and diligently collect and enforce payment of all Notes Receivable to the extent that it is commercially reasonable to do so and in a commercially reasonable manner" — against no benchmark. What collection or forbearance decisions breach the covenant cannot be determined from the clause.

The Borrowers must deliver policies endorsed "naming Lender as the sole loss payee (under a satisfactory lender's loss payable endorsement) or additional insured, as appropriate" without saying who decides what is appropriate or when each form is required. The scope of "all other hazards and risks as ordinarily are insured against by other Persons engaged in the same or similar businesses" is likewise left to be supplied from outside the clause.

This section permits the Borrower to "amend Schedule 5.5 and Schedule 5.7" on 30 days' notice, while Section 6.14 provides that no notification to Lender "shall ... have the effect of amending or modifying this Agreement or any of the Schedules hereto" and Section 15.1 requires every amendment to be signed by Lender. Whether a unilateral notice can change an incorporated schedule cannot be answered from this section alone.

The separateness covenants are enumerated as "(a) ... (c) ... and (d)", with no clause (b) anywhere in the section. Whether an obligation was dropped in drafting, and what the omitted item required, is a mechanical defect on the face of the covenant that is enforced without cure period under Section 8.2(a).

This section provides that no disclosure notification "shall ... have the effect of amending or modifying this Agreement or any of the Schedules hereto", yet Sections 5.8, 5.16, 5.18 and 5.21 describe their schedules as "updated from time to time" and Sections 2.6(c) and 6.9 expressly authorize the Borrowers to amend Schedules 2.6, 5.5 and 5.7. Whether a schedule can ever be updated, and to what effect, is a direct conflict.

The covenant requires delivery of "all original promissory notes and other documents" but only "[t]o the extent necessary to comply with Section 4.2", which itself requires only enough notes to keep a $250,000,000 pool with Lender. Whether the Borrower must deliver the whole portfolio or only the shortfall — and what "necessary" measures — is unresolved on the face of the clause.

Section 6.17 requires "all amounts delivered to any Borrower to be held in escrow ... on behalf of any Account Debtor" to be deposited into a Deposit Account subject to a perfected Lender's Lien, while Section 2.6(e) excludes from the Escrow Account regime "accounts belonging to an Account Debtor of Borrower". The two covenants give opposite answers for money held for an Account Debtor.

The covenant requires escrow instructions compelling delivery of "each of the documents listed in Section 3.3(z)", but Section 3.3 has no subsection (z) — its subsections run (a) through (f), and the document list is in Section 3.1(t). The obligation is tied to a cross-reference that does not exist.

The permitted-debt list does not include the Fund's redemption and return-of-capital obligations to its members, yet Section 8.9(x) expressly contemplates "capital obligations to any member or former member in connection with their Investor Membership Interests" and Schedule 5.8 discloses 50 pending redemption requests. Whether those obligations are prohibited Indebtedness under Section 7.1 or merely a cross-default trigger is unresolved between the two.

The covenant forbids suffering to exist "any Lien on or with respect to any of its assets, of any kind", and "Lien" is defined to include easements, rights-of-way, covenants, conditions and restrictions affecting Real Property. Read with that definition the covenant is breached by routine title exceptions unless clause (k) of "Permitted Liens" carries them, which depends on the undefined "materially interfere" standard.

Section 7.4 prohibits disposing of "any of a Borrower's or its Subsidiaries' assets" other than Permitted Dispositions, while Section 7.3(c) prohibits disposing only of "all or any substantial part of its assets" other than Permitted Dispositions. The two covenants set different thresholds for the same conduct, and which controls an ordinary-course sale is not stated.

The covenant forbids changing names, federal employer identification numbers, organizational identification numbers, state of organization or organizational identity, but the proviso relieves only name changes on 30 days' notice. On an expressio unius reading the other four changes are absolutely prohibited even with notice and new financing statements, which the proviso's closing words appear to assume.

The covenant bars suspending or changing "in any material respect the principal nature of its or their business" while carving out "the curtailment in the origination of new loans" — so ceasing to make loans altogether is or is not a change in the principal nature of a lending business depending on how far "curtailment" reaches. Neither "material respect" nor "curtailment" is defined.

Clause (c) forbids amending the terms of permitted Indebtedness "in any manner that would be adverse to any Borrower" — a covenant running for the protection of the covenantor rather than the Lender, which is the opposite of what every other clause of Section 7.7 does. Whether "Borrower" here should be read as "Lender" is a defect a court would be asked to construe.

This covenant bars material changes to the Required Procedures "without advance notice to, and consent by, the Lender", while the definition of "Borrower's Required Procedures" permits amendment only "with the prior written approval of Lender, which approval shall be given or withheld in Lender's sole discretion". Whether unwritten consent suffices, and how much advance notice is required, cannot be settled from this section alone.

The proviso permits Fund to distribute to holders of Investor Membership Interests "to the extent required or permitted by Fund's Governing Documents", handing the measure of a negative covenant to a document the Fund itself can amend, while clause (e) of the "Restricted Payments" definition captures any payment "not expressly authorized in this Agreement". The two cannot both be given effect.

The Investment covenant excepts "Permitted Investments" and anything "in connection with a Permitted Reorganization", but the definitions of "New Fund" and "Subsidiary" together take affiliated entities funded with debt securities outside the covenant structure entirely. Whether capitalizing or lending to such a fund is a prohibited Investment is only answerable by reading Section 7.12 with those definitions.

The opening prohibition on forming or acquiring "any Subsidiary without the prior written consent of Lender" is hollowed out by the proviso to the definition of "Subsidiary", which excludes any post-Closing entity not capitalized with Borrower assets, any New Fund, and Bar-K, Inc. Whether the covenant reaches the formation of an affiliated lending fund is a conflict between the two.

Clause (b)(ii) permits Advances to be used for "funding of its obligations with respect to any Investor Membership Interests or pursuant to a Permitted Reorganization", while Section 7.10 forbids Restricted Payments — defined to include any redemption or acquisition for value of Stock in a Borrower — except in narrow circumstances. Whether borrowed money may be used to redeem members cannot be decided without reconciling the two.

Clause (b) caps the Senior Leverage Ratio "(expressed as a percentage)" at "nine-tenths of one percent (0.9%)", which against the $600,000,000 Tangible Net Worth required by clause (a) permits only about $5.4 million of Obligations — far below the $50,000,000 "Maximum Revolver Amount" and the Borrowing Base of Section 2.1(a). The covenant and the credit facility cannot both be given effect as written.

The 25% cap is measured by reference to "Defaulted Notes Receivable", a term defined as any note that "Administrative Borrower or Lender deems to be non-performing or non-collectible". Whether the covenant is breached therefore depends on a subjective deeming by either party, and the two provisions read together make the financial covenant self-triggering at Lender's option.

Clause (a) makes immediate default out of a failure to observe "Sections ... 6.15 ...", but Section 6.15 of this Agreement is "[Intentionally Omitted]" and Section 6.4 is "Intentionally Blank" and appears nowhere in the list. A default clause keyed to an omitted covenant cannot be applied without construing the two together.

Default arises if "any material portion" of a Borrower's assets "comes into the possession of any third Person" — a phrase that, unqualified by any adverse-process requirement, would capture the original notes the Borrowers must deliver to Lender's custodian under Section 4.2 and files stored in a public warehouse under Section 7.15. Neither "material portion" nor "comes into the possession" is bounded.

Clause (x) makes it an Event of Default if the Fund defaults on "its capital obligations to any member or former member in connection with their Investor Membership Interests", yet Schedule 5.8 discloses 50 members with pending redemption requests that the Manager may honour or not "in the discretion of the Manager". Whether a deferred redemption is a default on a capital obligation cannot be answered without reading the clause against that schedule.

Default turns on whether a departed Executive Officer is replaced by "an individual with comparable education, experience and other qualifications acceptable to Lender" — a standard with no reasonableness limit and no procedure for approving a candidate. The clause also relies on the definition of "Executive Officer", which names individuals without identifying any "current position".

The clause defaults the loan if "[a]ny Borrower fails to comply, in any material respect, with its obligations under the Servicing Agreement", but the Servicing Agreement is defined as an agreement "between Borrower, Servicer and Lender" in which the servicing duties are the Servicer's — and Bar-K, Inc. is expressly not a Subsidiary of any Borrower. Whose non-performance triggers this default is unresolved between the clause and the definition.

The default is keyed to "[a]ny provision of any Loan Document that Lender in its Permitted Discretion deems to be material", combining an undefined materiality judgment with the lender-side "Permitted Discretion" standard. Which provisions of an open-ended set of Loan Documents can trigger it is left to the Lender's own determination.

The three-Business-Day cure operates only after "notice from Lender", yet Section 4.9(a) obliges Lender itself to return notes on repayment, which is the very act that can drop the pool below $250,000,000. Whether Lender's own releases can create the shortfall that defaults the Borrowers is unresolved between the two provisions.

Clauses (e) and (o) provide that amounts Lender incurs "shall be Lender Group Expenses", a term this Agreement never defines — the defined term is "Lender Expenses", and only that term is secured, chargeable to the Loan Account and first in the Section 2.3(b) waterfall. Whether those collection and servicing costs are recoverable at all turns on the undefined term.

Section 10 lets Lender, whenever a Borrower fails to pay taxes, insurance or rents, "set up such reserves against the Borrowing Base or the Maximum Revolver Amount as Lender deems necessary", with no Triggering Event condition and no Permitted Discretion standard. That cannot be squared with Section 2.1(b), where Lender "agrees not to establish any such reserves unless a Triggering Event has occurred and is continuing".

The capitalized sentence extends the indemnity to liabilities "CAUSED BY OR ARISE OUT OF ANY NEGLIGENT ACT OR OMISSION OF SUCH INDEMNIFIED PERSON", while the closing proviso withdraws it for "gross negligence or willful misconduct of such Indemnified Person". Where an ordinary-negligence claim by the Borrower itself falls between those two sentences is a construction question on the face of the section.

The deemed-receipt sentence provides that notices "shall be deemed received on the earlier of the date of actual receipt or three (3) Business Days after the deposit thereof in the mail ... and shall be as effective if sent by telefacsimile or other electronic transmission as notice or demand sent by any other method", which never states when a faxed or emailed notice is deemed received. For notices with cure periods running from receipt, the omission is operative.

New York law is made to govern construction and enforcement of the Agreement and the Loan Documents, but Sections 2.13(g) and 2.13(h) waive rights and defenses that exist only under California Code of Civil Procedure Sections 580a, 580b, 580d and 726, and all of the mortgage collateral lies in California and other states. Whether the choice of New York law leaves those waivers with anything to operate on is a whole-instrument question.

Assignments must be to Eligible Transferees "in a minimum amount of $5,000,000", but the closing sentence provides that "the Assignee need not be an Eligible Transferee" in a sale of the assigning Lender's business or loan portfolio without saying whether the $5,000,000 minimum also falls away. Which of the two requirements survives such a sale is left open.

The subsection says an assignment "shall effect a novation between Borrowers and the Assignee" and releases the assigning Lender "from any future obligations", while Section 14.2 provides that "[n]o consent to assignment by Lender shall release any Borrower from its Obligations" and the proviso here preserves surviving obligations. Whether a novation actually occurs, and what survives it, is unresolved between the two provisions.

This subsection deems the Agreement "amended to the extent ... necessary to reflect the addition of the Assignee" on the Administrative Borrower's mere receipt of the assignment, whereas Section 15.1 makes no amendment effective "unless the same shall be in writing and signed by Lender and Administrative Borrower". The two cannot both be given effect on an assignment.

Clause (v) deems each Participant "to have the right of set-off ... to the same extent as if the amount of its participating interest were owing directly to it as a Lender", while the closing sentences state that "no Participant shall have any rights under this Agreement or the other Loan Documents or any direct rights as to Borrowers". The subsection both grants and denies the Participant a direct right against the Borrowers.

Section 16.1 fixes effectiveness by execution but creates no "Effective Date", while the definition of "New Fund" turns on entities formed "after the Effective Date" and every other operative provision uses the "Closing Date". Which date the New Fund carve-out runs from can only be settled by reading the two together.

After saying headings are for convenience only, the section adds that "[u]nless the contrary is compelled by the context, everything contained in each Section applies equally to this entire Agreement" — a sentence that, read literally, would make every section-specific limitation (for example the reserve restriction in Section 2.1(b) or the priority rule in Section 2.3(b)(iv)) general. What that sentence means is a defect in its own words.

The severability clause makes each provision "severable from every other provision ... for the purpose of determining the legal enforceability of any specific provision" but never says what becomes of the Agreement if a provision is held unenforceable — whether it is struck, reformed, or the whole falls. The omission matters most for the California waivers in Section 2.13 and the prepayment premium.

A blanket bar on payment "without setoff, counterclaim, or other defense" is buried in a section captioned "Withholding Taxes" and otherwise devoted entirely to gross-up for Taxes. Whether that opening sentence is a free-standing waiver of all defenses to payment or is confined to tax-related payments is an ambiguity created by its placement and wording.

The integration clause makes the Agreement and the other Loan Documents the entire understanding, yet the definitions of "Permitted Reorganization" and "Borrower's Required Procedures" both make performance depend on unattached pre-closing writings delivered to Lender that are not Loan Documents. Whether those writings may be used to determine what the parties agreed cannot be answered from this section alone.

Each Borrower "irrevocably appoints Manager as the borrowing agent and attorney-in-fact", and the same sentence then provides that the appointment lasts "unless and until Lender shall have received prior written notice signed by each Borrower that such appointment has been revoked". An appointment that is both irrevocable and revocable on notice is self-contradictory on its face.

The form is a shell of blanks and unresolved bracketed alternatives — "commencing on the first day of ,20" and "[the first day of a month not less than 3 Business Days after the date of this Notice]" — so the notice does not itself state when a Base Rate election takes effect. Section 2.12(c) requires the election before the LIBOR Deadline, three Business Days before the Interest Period, and the bracketed text neither adopts nor displaces that timing.

Paragraph 2 certifies the representations true "except to the extent that such representations and warranties (x) relate solely to an earlier date or (y) relate to an action or omission permitted by Lender", while paragraph 5 certifies the same representations subject only to exceptions "set forth on Schedule 2". The certificate contains two differently qualified versions of one certification.

Paragraph 5 repeats the representation certification already given in paragraph 2 but with a different set of exceptions — Schedule 2 disclosure rather than Lender-permitted actions — so the officer certifies the same fact twice on inconsistent terms. Which qualification governs a disclosed breach is unresolved within the certificate.

The compliance certification is given as to "Sections 7.16, and 7.37 of the Loan Agreement", but the Agreement has no Section 7.37 — Section 7 ends at 7.17, which is the delinquent-and-defaulted-notes covenant that Section 6.3 requires the certificate to address. The certification is tied to a provision that does not exist.

The form leaves the commencement date blank — "commencing on the first day of 20" — and carries an unresolved bracketed instruction "[the first day of a month not less than 3 Business Days after the date of this Notice]", so the notice does not on its face fix the Interest Period it elects. Section 2.12(b) makes the LIBOR Deadline three Business Days before the Interest Period commences.

The notice "confirms Borrower's acceptance of the LIBOR Rate determined for the LIBOR Rate Advance for such Interest Period", but under the definition of "Base LIBOR Rate" that rate is fixed by Lender two Business Days before the Interest Period begins — after the notice is given three Business Days before. The borrower is made to accept in advance a rate not yet determined and "conclusive in the absence of manifest error".

The Designated Account Bank is Greater Bay Bank, while Section 2.6(a) provides that "[f]rom and after 60 days after the Closing Date ... Wells Fargo shall be the only Cash Management Bank and all of the Cash Management Accounts shall be maintained at Wells Fargo". Whether the Designated Account may remain outside Wells Fargo, given that Advance proceeds and Collections both pass through it, is not resolved between the schedule and Section 2.6.

The Designated Account is held by the Manager ("B-4 PARTNER, LLC"), yet Section 2.6(a)(ii) requires all Collections to be deposited into a Cash Management Account "in Fund's name" and Section 6.12(d) requires each Borrower not to commingle its funds with those of its Affiliates. Funding all Advances into the Manager's account sits against both requirements.

Lender's Account is "[a]n account at a bank designated by Lender from time to time", with no notice mechanism, while Section 2.7 provides that a payment is not received unless it reaches "the Lender's Account" and Section 2.3(a) requires payment there by 1:00 p.m. A borrower who pays to the last identified account after a unilateral change bears the consequences under provisions that do not address the change.

Item 1 permits a Fremont Bank lien on a $1,000,000 certificate of deposit, but the schedule does not "specifically identif[y]" that lien as entitled to priority over the Lender's Liens, which is the condition Section 2.1(b)(ii) imposes before Lender must refrain from reserving against such a lien. The schedule and Section 2.1(b) therefore give different answers on the same encumbrance.

The schedule discloses that redemptions occur in the ordinary course and that 50 members have pending redemption requests, while Section 5.8(b) represents that, except as described on the schedule, no Borrower "is subject to any obligation (contingent or otherwise) to repurchase or otherwise acquire or retire any of its capital Stock". Whether the schedule's narrative qualifies the representation or contradicts it — and how it stands with the Restricted Payments prohibition in Section 7.10 — is unresolved.

The schedule discloses that the maker of the Queen Mary loan is in Chapter 11 with adversary proceedings pending, which under clause (q) of the "Eligible Notes Receivable" definition makes that note ineligible and under the definition of "Defaulted Note Receivable" counts toward the Section 7.17 cap. Whether a litigation disclosure also operates as an eligibility concession is not addressed by either provision.

The schedule discloses a senior lienholder foreclosing on part of the property securing the Harmony Holding loan, which cannot be squared with Section 5.2(i) and clauses (b) and (h) of the "Eligible Notes Receivable" definition, both of which require each note to be secured by a first-priority, title-insured lien. Whether disclosure on Schedule 5.10 qualifies those representations is unresolved.
